Innings: 2
Fields:
- inn2.total_runs

Commentary:
At Northbay Cricket Oval in Eastport, this rewritten contest kept the same low-scoring chase architecture but moved every identifying scorecard fingerprint into a new structure, and the match belonged to Meadowridge Women because they were better at managing the awkward middle of both innings rather than because they ever blew Silverbank Women away in one dramatic burst. Silverbank chose to bat first and immediately found themselves working from an uncomfortable base, Nora Finch trapped lbw by Isla Rowan before the innings had properly settled, and although the score had moved only to two, the dismissal carried more weight than the number alone because it forced Emily Vale to start managing the innings almost from the first over. Chloe Hart gave Emily the first useful stretch of company, making fourteen from sixteen with two boundaries, and that second-wicket stand of twenty-six did exactly enough to stop the innings from becoming a complete powerplay mess. Still, it never truly shifted control to Silverbank, because Meadowridge kept the rate pinned down, Ivy Clarke bowled with real discipline, and when Chloe was taken after edging the innings toward the high twenties, Silverbank had to reset again. Mia Lawson did not last, Sara Brooks going through her for two, and at thirty-two for three the innings had the same kind of cramped, hesitant feel that often decides youth T20s: one batter set, several partners already gone, and every new arrival needing to rebuild before she could attack. Emily Vale and Sophie Lane handled that phase with the calm Silverbank badly needed. Their stand of thirty-nine was the center of the innings, not loud, not flashy, but structurally vital, because Emily’s thirty-four from thirty-eight gave Silverbank their one settled top-order hand while Sophie slowly built the base that would carry them to the end. The problem was that the stand used up time without ever becoming a launchpad. Meadowridge were content to let the innings advance in singles and controlled twos because they knew the boundaries were not coming often enough to damage the match. Leah Stone eventually removed Emily at seventy-one for four, and that was a key wicket because Silverbank had finally reached the point where the set batter could have started pushing harder. Instead, Sophie had to begin again with Grace Morton. Grace’s twelve from fourteen had use, and that partnership of twenty-four dragged the total into the mid-nineties, but Isla Rowan returned to remove her before the closing overs could become anything too uncomfortable. Lily Carter helped briefly, Eva Brooks struck her one scoring ball cleanly at the end, and Sophie Lane finished unbeaten on thirty-one from thirty-six, but Silverbank’s final total of one hundred and eight for six felt like a score built through resistance rather than authority. Meadowridge’s bowlers had done their job with precision. Isla Rowan took two wickets and made the early and late cuts. Ivy Clarke’s four overs for fourteen with a maiden gave the innings its squeeze. Sara Brooks allowed almost nothing loose. Leah Stone removed the set opener at the moment Silverbank needed acceleration. Mira Wells stopped Lily Carter before the last over could turn messy. The chase, though, was not effortless, and that is why Isla Rowan’s all-round performance matters so much. Meadowridge needed one hundred and nine, and the first stand between Hannah Cole and Lucy Grant moved them to twenty-one, but five of those runs came in extras, which already hinted that the chase was being helped by Silverbank’s looseness as much as by clean batting. Lucy was bowled by Lily Carter, Hannah was then run out, and Meadowridge were twenty-eight for two with the target still far enough away to leave the game unsettled. Isla Rowan, already central with the ball, now became central with the bat. She did not play a reckless chase. She played a controlled one, and that distinction mattered because Silverbank were defending a small total and needed panic more than anything else. Zoe Mercer helped her through the most important middle passage, a stand of thirty that took Meadowridge to fifty-eight, but Zoe was run out by Emily Vale just when the innings was beginning to look calmer. Maya Scott then failed to score, caught behind off Eva Brooks, and at sixty-six for four the match had one last possible route back toward Silverbank. That was the point where Isla showed why she was the correct player of the match. She stayed there, kept the chase organized, and found the one partner who could finish it with her. Leah Stone’s unbeaten eighteen from eleven was the sharp support hand the chase needed, especially after Meadowridge had lost four wickets and could not afford to drift. The final stand of forty-three did not feel like a wild assault; it felt like the gradual closing of a door. Isla picked the safer scoring options, took the boundary ball when it arrived, and let the extra runs Silverbank kept giving away reduce the pressure even further. Leah added enough pace at the other end to stop the chase from becoming a final-over crawl. Silverbank’s bowling had individual merit, especially Lily Carter’s four overs for twelve and Eva Brooks’ controlled spell, but the extras hurt them badly, with nine wides and four leg byes making a modest target smaller every over. By the time Meadowridge reached one hundred and nine for four at the end of the nineteenth over, the result felt earned rather than easy. Silverbank had fought through Emily Vale and Sophie Lane, then defended with enough discipline in patches to make the chase slightly awkward, but Meadowridge had the one player who connected both halves of the match. Isla Rowan took two wickets when Silverbank were trying to build, then batted through the chase from uncertainty to completion. That is why Meadowridge won by six wickets: they did not dominate every phase, but they controlled the most important ones, and in a low-scoring game that was enough.
